a010_t10_orig_b004_l1e-05 | -103,821 ★ | Optimal | Maximilian Schicker | Classical | 2025-08-19 | 0.87 | 1

13 | Two problems, judged on scale and quality

THE CHALLENGE

QOBLIB 06 · Notebook 01 — Portfolio optimisation
Multi-period, with transaction costs.
58 to ~36,000 binary variables across the instances.

QOBLIB 08 · Notebook 02 — Network design
Degree-constrained topology with traffic routing.
20 to 552 binary variables across the instances.

How the winner is chosen
- Scale: the largest instance you reach.
- Quality: QOBLIB's official objective, compared with the best published results.

Run notebook 00 first, then one of 01 or 02. The Handing in section of notebook 00
says what to submit.

14 | Multi-period portfolio optimisation

PROBLEM A · QOBLIB 06

- You decide: How many units of each asset to hold, long or short, in each period.
- Objective: Balance expected return against risk, net of the transaction costs
  of changing positions.
- Constraints: 0 to 3 units per asset and direction, plus capital and budget
  limits each period.
- Size: Integer holdings become groups of binaries: 58 to ~36,000 variables.

Where the couplings are
- Risk links assets within the same period.
- Transaction costs link each asset to itself in the next period.
- Cutting by period drops transaction-cost links; cutting by asset group drops
  risk links. Measure which loses less.

Notebook 01: official model → QUBO → classical baseline → PCE and partitioned
QAOA → solution file

15 | Network design

PROBLEM B · QOBLIB 08

- You decide: Which directed links to build between n nodes: exactly 2 out and
  2 in per node.
- Then: Route the traffic demand between every pair of nodes over the links you built.
- Objective: Minimise the load on the busiest link.
- Size: One binary per possible link, n(n−1): 20 at 5 nodes, 552 at 24 nodes.

How the work is split
- Quantum: a topology QUBO, with the degree rules as Divi LinearConstraints.
- Classical: an exact routing LP scores each sampled topology.
- Each degree rule ties together one node's row or column of links. A cut through
  a row leaves that rule for stitching to enforce.

Notebook 02: topology QUBO → sample → route with LP → score → solution file

16 | How solutions are scored

THE CHALLENGE

PROBLEM A · PORTFOLIO OPTIMISATION
- Rules the referee checks: 0 to 3 units per asset and direction; capital and
  budget limits in every period.
- Score: Risk minus return, plus transaction, short-selling and liquidation costs,
  minus interest on cash.

PROBLEM B · NETWORK DESIGN
- Rules the referee checks: Every node has exactly 2 links out and 2 in; flows
  deliver all the demand over chosen links only.
- Score: The largest total flow on any link, in units of 1/1000.

Quality: your gap to the best-known value
gap = (score − best) / |best|
0% matches the best-known value; below 0% beats it. Example: −69,169 against
−69,482 is a 0.45% gap.

Scale
The binary variables in the instance you solve, and the qubits in your largest
quantum program.

Lower is better for both problems. A solution that breaks a rule doesn't count,
and the referee recomputes the objective from your .sol file.

17 | Prizes

THE CHALLENGE

- 1st place: 2 months, 50,000 platform credits, a guided project of your choice
  with support from the Qoro team, and Qoro T-shirts.
- 2nd place: 20,000 platform credits and Qoro T-shirts.
- 3rd place: 5,000 platform credits and Qoro T-shirts.

18 | Getting started

THE CHALLENGE

01. Sign up at dash.qoroquantum.net. Get your API key and hackathon credits.
02. Open the challenge template at aqora.io/qoro/pushquantum-2026-template.
    The notebooks, setup and how to hand in. Or on GitHub:
    github.com/QoroQuantum/pushquantum-hackathon-2026
03. Join #pushquantumhack-26 on Slack for help, Q&A and announcements.

[Slack QR code and embedded invite link]
https://join.slack.com/t/qoroq/shared_invite/zt-3bpzfatnb-4QS4u2nwEAFRiXN3RAIf~g

Using an AI coding assistant? Give it Divi's docs: context7.com/qoroquantum/divi

Setup for Colab and local runs is on the next slide.

19 | Setup: Colab or your own machine

THE CHALLENGE

In Google Colab
1. Open a notebook with its Open in Colab badge.
2. Add a Colab secret named QORO_API_KEY and switch on notebook access.
3. Run the first setup cell. If it installs Divi 0.16.2, restart the session and
   run again.
4. File › Save a copy in Drive to keep your changes.

On your own machine

    git clone https://github.com/QoroQuantum/pushquantum-hackathon-2026.git
    cd pushquantum-hackathon-2026
    pip install "qoro-divi[qubo-decompose,jupyter]==0.16.2"

Python 3.11 or newer. Put QORO_API_KEY="your key" in a .env file next to the
notebooks; .gitignore keeps it out of commits.
Optional: pip install qiskit-maestro or pennylane-maestro for your own Qiskit or
PennyLane code.

No API key yet? Everything runs on the local simulator, and cloud-only cells
(the Characterization Service) print Skipped.

20 | The starter kit: three notebooks and a referee

THE CHALLENGE

- Start here — Notebook 00: Setup, QUBO 101 with Divi, picking a problem and
  handing in. About 1–4 min.
- Problem A — Notebook 01: Portfolio optimisation: official model, QUBO,
  classical baseline, then PCE and partitioned QAOA. About 6 min.
- Problem B — Notebook 02: Network design: topology QUBO with Divi
  LinearConstraints and an exact routing LP, then sample and score. About 7 min.
- The referee — qoblib_tools.py: Instance loaders, official scorers, QUBO
  builders and .sol writers. Don't edit it. Referee for 01 and 02.

Run order: notebook 00 first, then one of 01 or 02. Times are for one run on a
12-core Mac; most of it is the Characterization Service calls, and Colab is slower.

Classical repair and local search are strong: compare every quantum result with
the notebooks' baselines before claiming a quantum contribution.

github.com/QoroQuantum/pushquantum-hackathon-2026

21 | Notebook 00: QUBO 101 with Divi

THE CHALLENGE

Part 0 — Setup
API key, install, and backend: the local simulator, or Qoro's cloud with
USE_CLOUD = True.

Part 1 — QUBO 101 with Divi
1. Build a QUBO.
2. Characterize and validate it.
3. QAOA, blind and warm-started.
4. Pauli Correlation Encoding (PCE).
5. Partitioning.

Part 2 — Your problem
Choose portfolio or network design, run it in Colab, and see exactly what to hand in.

Setup is explained only in notebook 00 and the README; notebooks 01 and 02 repeat
the setup code without the explanations.

22 | Let's build

PUSHQUANTUM 2026

14 | Multi-period portfolio optimisation

PROBLEM A · QOBLIB 06

  of changing positions.

  limits each period.
- Size: Integer holdings become groups of binaries: 58 to ~36,000 variables.

Where the couplings are
- Risk links assets within the same period.
- Transaction costs link each asset to itself in the next period.
- Cutting by period drops transaction-cost links; cutting by asset group drops
  risk links. Measure which loses less.

QAOA → solution file

15 | Network design

  2 in per node.

- Size: One binary per possible link, n(n−1): 20 at 5 nodes, 552 at 24 nodes.

How the work is split
- Quantum: a topology QUBO, with the degree rules as Divi LinearConstraints.
- Classical: an exact routing LP scores each sampled topology.
- Each degree rule ties together one node's row or column of links. A cut through
  a row leaves that rule for stitching to enforce.

PROBLEM A · PORTFOLIO OPTIMISATION

  budget limits in every period.

  minus interest on cash.

PROBLEM B · NETWORK DESIGN
- Rules the referee checks: Every node has exactly 2 links out and 2 in; flows
  deliver all the demand over chosen links only.
- Score: The largest total flow on any link, in units of 1/1000.

Quality: your gap to the best-known value
gap = (score − best) / |best|
0% matches the best-known value; below 0% beats it. Example: −69,169 against
−69,482 is a 0.45% gap.

Scale
The binary variables in the instance you solve, and the qubits in your largest
quantum program.

Lower is better for both problems. A solution that breaks a rule doesn't count,
and the referee recomputes the objective from your .sol file.

# Qoro × PushQuantum Hackathon — 02 · Network design (QOBLIB 08)

[![Open In Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/assets/colab-badge.svg)](https://colab.research.google.com/github/QoroQuantum/pushquantum-hackathon-2026/blob/main/02_network_design.ipynb)

Build a directed network in which every node has exactly two outgoing and two incoming links, so that
when all traffic is routed, the busiest link carries as little as possible. A QUBO proposes network
topologies, and an exact linear program scores them. This notebook builds that pipeline, compares
quantum and classical proposers, and writes a solution file in QOBLIB's format.

**Your challenge: scale up.** Instances run from `network05` (20 binary variables) to `network24`
(552). Up to `network10` the optimum is proven; from `network11` on, only best-known values exist
(section 1.5). Solve the largest instance you can, as close to the best-known value as you can.

**Scoring** uses QOBLIB's official objective, not your QUBO's energy: `qt.route_min_congestion`
reproduces every published QOBLIB value. Treat it as the referee.

**Before you start,** work through notebook 00 (setup and QUBO 101).

def solve_partitioned(bqm, routine="qaoa", cluster_size=12, n_layers=2, backend=backend, decomposer=None, **routine_kwargs):
    # Partition `bqm`, solve every part with `routine`, and return the ensemble.
    # routine: "qaoa" | "iterative_qaoa" | "pce" | "progressive_pce"
    problem = BinaryOptimizationProblem(
        bqm,
        decomposer=decomposer or CommunityDecomposer(
            QUBOPartitioningConfig(max_n_variables_per_cluster=cluster_size)
        ),
        composer=hybrid.SplatComposer(),
        local_search=True,
    )
    ensemble = PartitioningProgramEnsemble(
        problem=problem,
        quantum_routine=routine,
        n_layers=n_layers,
        optimizer=MonteCarloOptimizer(population_size=MC_POPULATION),
        max_iterations=MC_ITERATIONS,
        backend=backend,
        **routine_kwargs,
    )
    ensemble.run()
    return ensemble
=== cell 8 markdown
---
## 1 · QOBLIB 08: network design

Given an $n \times n$ traffic demand matrix $t_{ij}$, build a directed network on $n$ nodes in which
**every node has exactly 2 outgoing and 2 incoming links** (no self-loops). Route all traffic, letting
flows split over several paths, and **minimise the largest total flow on any link**. The score is that
maximum × 1000, as an integer. Instances `network05` … `network24` use the top-left $n \times n$
block of one fixed demand matrix.

The problem splits into two parts (credit to the parallel-tempering submission on QOBLIB):

* **Choosing the topology** is combinatorial: one binary variable per possible link, $n(n-1)$ in
  total. This is the QUBO part.
* **Routing on a fixed topology** is a linear program that `qt.route_min_congestion` solves exactly in
  milliseconds. It reproduces every published QOBLIB value.

So the quantum or QUBO solver *proposes* topologies, and the LP *scores* them.

print("Its score:", qt.route_min_congestion(demand, ref_arcs).objective)
print("A random valid topology:", qt.route_min_congestion(demand, qt.random_topology(N_NODES, np.random.default_rng(0))).objective)
=== cell 10 markdown
For `network05` there are few enough topologies to score every one, giving a ground truth for the
pipeline below.
=== cell 11 code
rows = [list(itertools.combinations([j for j in range(N_NODES) if j != i], 2)) for i in range(N_NODES)]
all_topologies = []
for choice in itertools.product(*rows):
    arcs = [(i, j) for i, pair in enumerate(choice) for j in pair]
    if qt.is_valid_topology(N_NODES, arcs):
        all_topologies.append(arcs)
all_scores = np.array([qt.route_min_congestion(demand, a).objective for a in all_topologies])

=== cell 12 markdown
### 1.1 A topology QUBO with Divi's `LinearConstraint`

`qt.build_network_qubo` gives a **surrogate** objective. It rewards links that carry their own demand
directly: $-\sum t_{ij} x_{ij}$, scaled. The real objective needs the LP and is not a QUBO, so
**designing a better surrogate is a big part of the challenge.**

The degree rules are linear equalities. Instead of hand-building penalties, hand them to Divi as
`LinearConstraint`s: `BinaryOptimizationProblem` adds them as squared penalties, and
`problem.is_feasible(bitstring)` checks them. QAOA's `get_top_solutions(feasibility="filter")` keeps
only the feasible samples, ranked by the true objective rather than the penalised one.
=== cell 13 code
surrogate, degree_penalty, arcs = qt.build_network_qubo(demand)  # arcs[v] = link of variable v
constraints = []
for node in range(N_NODES):
    constraints.append(LinearConstraint({v: 1 for v, (i, j) in enumerate(arcs) if i == node}, "==", 2))  # out
    constraints.append(LinearConstraint({v: 1 for v, (i, j) in enumerate(arcs) if j == node}, "==", 2))  # in
net_problem = BinaryOptimizationProblem(surrogate, constraints=constraints, penalty_weight=2.0)
print(f"{len(arcs)} binary variables → {net_problem.cost_hamiltonian.num_qubits} qubits")
=== cell 14 markdown
### 1.2 Characterize & validate, then run QAOA

Before spending circuits, send `net_problem` to the **Characterization Service** (notebook 00, section
1.2) with the **published optimal topology as the reference state**. That validates the surrogate: if
the true optimum sits high in the QUBO's energy landscape, no sampler will find it through this QUBO,
and the surrogate needs work. On `network05` the published optimum is the QUBO's ground state.

The constraints count as the penalty component, so the report has a `penalty` section with a
recommended weight, and its `structure` section lists the ten degree rules as *penalty blocks*: groups
of 4 variables that must hold exactly 2 links each. The call can take several minutes. Divi warns that
the QUBO's constant offset isn't sent: the reported energies exclude it, and nothing else changes.

def run_network_qaoa(label, n_layers, initial_params=None):
    t0 = time.time()
    qaoa_net = QAOA(
        net_problem,
        n_layers=n_layers,
        optimizer=MonteCarloOptimizer(population_size=MC_POPULATION),
        max_iterations=MC_ITERATIONS,
        backend=make_backend(shots=20_000),
        seed=3,
    )
    qaoa_net.run(initial_params=initial_params)
    valid = qaoa_net.get_top_solutions(n=0, feasibility="filter")  # n=0: every feasible sample
    scores = {s.bitstring: qt.route_min_congestion(demand, qt.decode_topology(s.bitstring, arcs)).objective for s in valid}
    p_opt = sum(s.prob for s in valid if scores[s.bitstring] == all_scores.min())
    best = min(scores.values())
    print(f"{label:<24} {qaoa_net.total_circuit_count:>3} circuits, {time.time() - t0:>3.0f}s | {len(valid)} valid topologies, "
          f"{sum(s.prob for s in valid):5.1%} of the probability mass | P(optimal topology) {p_opt:.3%} | "
          f"best sampled: {best:.0f}, rank {(all_scores < best).sum() + 1} of {len(all_topologies)}")


run_network_qaoa("QAOA p=2, blind", n_layers=2)
init = net_report.qaoa_initial_params() if net_report is not None else None
if init is not None:

| Instance | Variables | Best known | Status |

| `network24` | 552 | 663 688 | best known (reference) |

**Ideas to try**
* **Better surrogates.** Reward two-hop paths $x_{ij}x_{jk}$ for large $t_{ik}$. Penalise nodes that
  send a lot of traffic over few links. Learn the weights from LP results.
* **LP feedback (Benders-style).** The LP's dual values tell you which links are congested. Re-weight
  the QUBO and re-solve in a loop.
* **Feasible-by-construction encodings.** A valid topology is two permutations with no fixed points
  that never agree. One-hot permutation encodings with an XY mixer keep QAOA inside the feasible space. The report in section 1.2 suggests the same: an XY mixer over each
  penalty block, started from a state with 2 links.
* **Beat SA first.** On `network12` the plain quantum pipelines above are far from the best known
  value, and simulated annealing on the same surrogate is a strong bar. Closing that gap with better surrogates, penalties, depth or encodings is a good first goal.
* **Quantum proposals inside a local search.** Use QAOA or PCE samples to propose degree-preserving
  2-exchanges, $(a\to b), (c\to d) \Rightarrow (a\to d), (c\to b)$, scored by the LP.
* **Characterize at scale.** Section 1.2 characterizes `network05`. Do the same for the instance you
  are pushing: read `structure` to choose partitions and `penalty` for the weight, and pass your best
  topology as a reference state to check that your surrogate ranks it well.

def solve_partitioned(bqm, routine="qaoa", cluster_size=12, n_layers=2, backend=backend, decomposer=None, **routine_kwargs):
    # Partition `bqm`, solve every part with `routine`, and return the ensemble.
    # routine: "qaoa" | "iterative_qaoa" | "pce" | "progressive_pce"
    problem = BinaryOptimizationProblem(
        bqm,
        decomposer=decomposer or CommunityDecomposer(
            QUBOPartitioningConfig(max_n_variables_per_cluster=cluster_size)
        ),
        composer=hybrid.SplatComposer(),
        local_search=True,
    )
    ensemble = PartitioningProgramEnsemble(
        problem=problem,
        quantum_routine=routine,
        n_layers=n_layers,
        optimizer=MonteCarloOptimizer(population_size=MC_POPULATION),
        max_iterations=MC_ITERATIONS,
        backend=backend,
        **routine_kwargs,
    )
    ensemble.run()
    return ensemble

## 1 · QOBLIB 08: network design

Given an $n \times n$ traffic demand matrix $t_{ij}$, build a directed network on $n$ nodes in which
**every node has exactly 2 outgoing and 2 incoming links** (no self-loops). Route all traffic, letting
flows split over several paths, and **minimise the largest total flow on any link**. The score is that
maximum × 1000, as an integer. Instances `network05` … `network24` use the top-left $n \times n$
block of one fixed demand matrix.

The problem splits into two parts (credit to the parallel-tempering submission on QOBLIB):

* **Choosing the topology** is combinatorial: one binary variable per possible link, $n(n-1)$ in
  total. This is the QUBO part.
* **Routing on a fixed topology** is a linear program that `qt.route_min_congestion` solves exactly in
  milliseconds. It reproduces every published QOBLIB value.

So the quantum or QUBO solver *proposes* topologies, and the LP *scores* them.

### 1.1 A topology QUBO with Divi's `LinearConstraint`

`qt.build_network_qubo` gives a **surrogate** objective. It rewards links that carry their own demand
directly: $-\sum t_{ij} x_{ij}$, scaled. The real objective needs the LP and is not a QUBO, so
**designing a better surrogate is a big part of the challenge.**

The degree rules are linear equalities. Instead of hand-building penalties, hand them to Divi as
`LinearConstraint`s: `BinaryOptimizationProblem` adds them as squared penalties, and
`problem.is_feasible(bitstring)` checks them. QAOA's `get_top_solutions(feasibility="filter")` keeps
only the feasible samples, ranked by the true objective rather than the penalised one.
=== cell 13 code
surrogate, degree_penalty, arcs = qt.build_network_qubo(demand)  # arcs[v] = link of variable v
constraints = []
for node in range(N_NODES):
    constraints.append(LinearConstraint({v: 1 for v, (i, j) in enumerate(arcs) if i == node}, "==", 2))  # out
    constraints.append(LinearConstraint({v: 1 for v, (i, j) in enumerate(arcs) if j == node}, "==", 2))  # in
net_problem = BinaryOptimizationProblem(surrogate, constraints=constraints, penalty_weight=2.0)
print(f"{len(arcs)} binary variables → {net_problem.cost_hamiltonian.num_qubits} qubits")

"""Network design (QOBLIB 08): secure a checked submission, then bank every improvement.

    python network_pipeline.py verify                    # network05 against the proven optimum
    python network_pipeline.py search 24 --minutes 10    # improve network24, banking as it goes
    python network_pipeline.py status                    # re-check every banked .sol file

Every candidate topology is scored by the exact routing LP. A topology is banked only after
integer flows are written to a .sol file and that file passes ``qt.check_network_solution``
with a strictly better score than the file already banked. ``qoblib_tools.py`` stays untouched.

The search is a degree-preserving 2-exchange local search, (a→b),(c→d) ⇒ (a→d),(c→b), with
moves biased towards congested links via the LP's dual values. The proposer is a plain function
(``propose_moves``) so a Divi-based proposer can replace it later.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import csv
import math
import os
import time
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor
from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import linprog

import qoblib_tools as qt

SOL_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent / "solutions"
LOG_PATH = SOL_DIR / "log.csv"

# Best-known values from QOBLIB's 08-network/solutions/README.md (lower is better).
BKV = {
    5: 65500, 6: 101000, 7: 142400, 8: 170231, 9: 196750, 10: 210800,
    11: 238334, 12: 276474, 13: 300620, 14: 343091, 15: 370870, 16: 397908,
    17: 437000, 18: 473375, 19: 492924, 20: 528528, 21: 569273, 22: 618135,
    23: 659369, 24: 663688,
}
PROVEN_OPTIMAL = set(range(5, 11))

Arc = tuple[int, int]


def gap(n: int, score: float) -> float:
    return (score - BKV[n]) / abs(BKV[n])


# ── Scoring ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

_DEMAND: np.ndarray | None = None


def _init_worker(demand: np.ndarray) -> None:
    global _DEMAND
    _DEMAND = demand


def score_topology(arcs: list[Arc], demand: np.ndarray | None = None) -> tuple[float, np.ndarray | None]:
    """Exact LP congestion (fractional, 1/1000 units) and per-arc duals, arcs in sorted order.

    Same LP as ``qt.route_min_congestion``; the referee's score is ``ceil`` of the first value.
    The duals say how much each link's capacity row binds: large dual = congested link.
    """
    demand = _DEMAND if demand is None else demand
    arcs = sorted(arcs)
    _, c, A_ub, A_eq, b_eq = qt._routing_lp(demand, arcs)
    res = linprog(c, A_ub=A_ub, b_ub=np.zeros(A_ub.shape[0]), A_eq=A_eq, b_eq=b_eq,
                  bounds=(0, None), method="highs")
    if res.status != 0:
        return math.inf, None
    return float(res.fun), -np.asarray(res.ineqlin.marginals)


# ── Banking ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

def banked_path(n: int) -> Path:
    return SOL_DIR / f"network{n:02d}.sol"


def banked_score(n: int, demand: np.ndarray) -> int | None:
    """Score of the banked file according to the checker (None if absent or invalid)."""
    path = banked_path(n)
    if not path.exists():
        return None
    valid, score, _ = qt.check_network_solution(path, n, demand)
    return score if valid else None


def bank(n: int, demand: np.ndarray, arcs: list[Arc], method: str) -> tuple[bool, int, str]:
    """Write integer flows for ``arcs``, check the file, keep it only if it beats the bank.

    Returns ``(banked, checked_score, message)``.
    """
    SOL_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    routing = qt.route_integral(demand, arcs)
    if routing.flows is None:
        return False, -1, "unroutable topology"
    tmp = SOL_DIR / f".network{n:02d}.candidate.sol"
    qt.write_network_solution(tmp, n, routing)
    valid, score, msg = qt.check_network_solution(tmp, n, demand)
    if not valid:
        tmp.unlink()
        return False, -1, f"checker rejected the file: {msg}"
    prev = banked_score(n, demand)
    if prev is not None and score >= prev:
        tmp.unlink()
        return False, score, f"checked {score}, not better than banked {prev}"
    tmp.replace(banked_path(n))
    new_log = not LOG_PATH.exists()
    with LOG_PATH.open("a", newline="") as f:
        w = csv.writer(f)
        if new_log:
            w.writerow(["timestamp", "instance", "variables", "score", "best_known", "gap", "method"])
        w.writerow([datetime.now().isoformat(timespec="seconds"), f"network{n:02d}", n * (n - 1),
                    score, BKV[n], f"{gap(n, score):.4%}", method])
    return True, score, f"banked {score} (gap {gap(n, score):+.3%}, was {prev})"


# ── Proposals ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

def swap(arcs: list[Arc], p: int, q: int) -> list[Arc] | None:
    """2-exchange of arcs p=(a,b) and q=(c,d) → (a,d),(c,b); None if it breaks the rules."""
    (a, b), (c, d) = arcs[p], arcs[q]
    if a == c or b == d or a == d or c == b:
        return None
    present = set(arcs)
    if (a, d) in present or (c, b) in present:
        return None
    new = list(arcs)
    new[p], new[q] = (a, d), (c, b)
    return sorted(new)


def propose_moves(arcs: list[Arc], duals: np.ndarray, k: int, rng: np.random.Generator,
                  bias: float = 0.7) -> list[list[Arc]]:
    """Up to ``k`` distinct neighbours. With probability ``bias`` the first arc is drawn in
    proportion to its LP dual (congested links first), otherwise uniformly."""
    m = len(arcs)
    w = np.clip(duals, 0, None) + 1e-12
    w = w / w.sum()
    seen, out = set(), []
    for _ in range(20 * k):
        if len(out) >= k:
            break
        p = rng.choice(m, p=w) if rng.random() < bias else rng.integers(m)
        q = rng.integers(m)

def propose_moves(arcs: list[Arc], duals: np.ndarray, k: int, rng: np.random.Generator,
                  bias: float = 0.7) -> list[list[Arc]]:
    """Up to ``k`` distinct neighbours. With probability ``bias`` the first arc is drawn in
    proportion to its LP dual (congested links first), otherwise uniformly."""
    m = len(arcs)
    w = np.clip(duals, 0, None) + 1e-12
    w = w / w.sum()
    seen, out = set(), []
    for _ in range(20 * k):
        if len(out) >= k:
            break
        p = rng.choice(m, p=w) if rng.random() < bias else rng.integers(m)
        q = rng.integers(m)
        new = swap(arcs, int(p), int(q))
        if new is not None and (key := tuple(new)) not in seen:
            seen.add(key)
            out.append(new)
    return out


# ── Search ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

def search(n: int, minutes: float, seed: int, batch: int, workers: int,
           start: str = "greedy", t0: float = 3000.0, t1: float = 30.0, patience: int = 400,
           verbose: bool = True) -> tuple[float, list[Arc]]:
    demand = qt.load_network_demand(n)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    if start == "banked" and banked_path(n).exists():
        _, cur, _ = qt.read_network_solution(banked_path(n))
    elif start == "random":
        cur = qt.random_topology(n, rng)
    else:  # links with the most direct demand
        cur = qt.repair_topology(n, [], demand)
    cur = sorted(cur)
    cur_z, cur_d = score_topology(cur, demand)
    best_z, best = cur_z, cur
    ok, score, msg = bank(n, demand, best, f"search start={start} seed={seed}")
    banked = banked_score(n, demand)
    if verbose:
        print(f"network{n:02d}: start ({start}) LP {cur_z:.0f} → {msg}")

    deadline = time.time() + 60 * minutes
    t_start, step, since_best = time.time(), 0, 0
    with ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=workers, initializer=_init_worker, initargs=(demand,)) as pool:
        while time.time() < deadline:
            frac = (time.time() - t_start) / (deadline - t_start)
            temp = t0 * (t1 / t0) ** frac
            cands = propose_moves(cur, cur_d, batch, rng)
            if not cands:
                break
            results = list(pool.map(score_topology, cands, chunksize=max(1, len(cands) // workers)))
            i = int(np.argmin([z for z, _ in results]))
            z, d = results[i]
            if z <= cur_z or rng.random() < math.exp(-(z - cur_z) / temp):
                cur, cur_z, cur_d = cands[i], z, d
            step += 1
            since_best += 1
            if cur_z < best_z - 1e-6:
                best_z, best, since_best = cur_z, cur, 0
                if banked is None or math.ceil(best_z - 1e-6) < banked:
                    ok, score, msg = bank(n, demand, best, f"search start={start} seed={seed} step={step}")
                    if ok:
                        banked = score
                    if verbose:
                        print(f"  step {step:>5}  T={temp:7.1f}  LP {best_z:.0f}  {msg}")
            if since_best >= patience:  # restart from the best topology found so far
                cur, cur_z = best, best_z
                cur_d = score_topology(cur, demand)[1]
                since_best = 0
    if verbose:
        el = time.time() - t_start
        print(f"network{n:02d}: {step} steps in {el:.0f}s, best LP {best_z:.0f}, "
              f"banked {banked} (gap {gap(n, banked):+.3%} vs {BKV[n]})")
    return best_z, best


# ── Commands ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

def cmd_verify(args) -> None:
    """network05: referee on the published optimum, then the full pipeline from a random start."""
    n = 5
    demand = qt.load_network_demand(n)
    ref = qt.fetch_qoblib_file(f"08-network/solutions/network{n:02d}.opt.sol")
    print("checker on the published optimum:", qt.check_network_solution(ref, n, demand))
    best_z, best = search(n, minutes=args.minutes, seed=args.seed, batch=8, workers=2,
                          start="random", verbose=False)
    score = banked_score(n, demand)
    status = "OK" if score == BKV[n] else "MISMATCH"
    print(f"pipeline on network05: LP {best_z:.0f}, banked file checks at {score}, "
          f"proven optimum {BKV[n]} → {status}")


def cmd_search(args) -> None:
    search(args.n, args.minutes, args.seed, args.batch, args.workers, start=args.start,
           t0=args.t0, t1=args.t1, patience=args.patience)


def cmd_status(args) -> None:
    files = sorted(SOL_DIR.glob("network[0-9][0-9].sol"))
    if not files:
        print("nothing banked yet")
    for path in files:
        n = int(path.stem[-2:])
        valid, score, msg = qt.check_network_solution(path, n, qt.load_network_demand(n))
        tag = "proven optimum" if n in PROVEN_OPTIMAL else "best known"
        line = f"{path.name}: {msg}, score {score}" if valid else f"{path.name}: INVALID ({msg})"
        if valid:
            line += f", {tag} {BKV[n]}, gap {gap(n, score):+.3%}"
        print(line)


def main() -> None:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__, formatter_class=argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter)
    sub = ap.add_subparsers(dest="cmd", required=True)
    v = sub.add_parser("verify", help="network05 against the proven optimum")
    v.add_argument("--minutes", type=float, default=0.2)
    v.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=0)
    v.set_defaults(func=cmd_verify)
    s = sub.add_parser("search", help="local search on one instance, banking every checked improvement")
    s.add_argument("n", type=int, choices=sorted(BKV))
    s.add_argument("--minutes", type=float, default=10)
    s.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=0)
    s.add_argument("--batch", type=int, default=32, help="candidate moves scored in parallel per step")
    s.add_argument("--workers", type=int, default=max(1, (os.cpu_count() or 2) - 1))
    s.add_argument("--start", choices=["greedy", "random", "banked"], default="greedy")
    s.add_argument("--t0", type=float, default=3000.0, help="initial temperature (1/1000 flow units)")
    s.add_argument("--t1", type=float, default=30.0, help="final temperature")
    s.add_argument("--patience", type=int, default=400, help="steps without improvement before a restart")
    s.set_defaults(func=cmd_search)
    st = sub.add_parser("status", help="re-check every banked .sol file")
    st.set_defaults(func=cmd_status)
    args = ap.parse_args()
    args.func(args)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Ho un network24.sol valido per il checker con punteggio **684 455**, cioè un gap del **+3,13%** dal best known di 663 688. Il primo passo del piano è fatto. Lo stesso processo, provato su network05, arriva all'ottimo dimostrato di 65 500.

| Istanza | Punteggio (checker) | Riferimento | Gap |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| network05 | 65 500 | 65 500 (ottimo dimostrato) | 0,000% |
| network24 | 684 455 | 663 688 (best known) | +3,129% |

**Come funziona [network_pipeline.py](network_pipeline.py):**
- **Topologia iniziale:** sceglie i link con più traffico diretto e parte da 768 375.
- **Ricerca locale:** prova molte volte a scambiare le destinazioni di due link, (a→b),(c→d) ⇒ (a→d),(c→b), il che lascia ogni nodo con 2 link in uscita e 2 in entrata. Ogni topologia proposta viene valutata con il routing LP esatto. Gli scambi che toccano i link più congestionati (indicati dai valori duali dell'LP) vengono provati più spesso.
- **Salvataggio:** quando trova una topologia migliore, calcola i flussi interi, scrive il `.sol` e lo rilegge col checker. Il file in `solutions/` viene sostituito solo se è valido e strettamente migliore, e ogni miglioramento va in `solutions/log.csv`.
- **Comandi:** `verify` rifà il test su network05, `search 24 --minutes N --start banked` riparte dal file salvato, `status` ricontrolla tutti i file salvati.

**Il limite:** la ricerca locale si blocca presto. La corsa da 10 minuti è scesa da 686 000 a 684 455 al passo 12, poi non ha più migliorato in quasi 2 400 passi. Il primo miglioramento di questa ricerca deve far cambiare più link insieme, non uno scambio alla volta. Al momento ripartire dalla migliore soluzione trovata riporta la ricerca allo stesso punto. Questo è il ruolo previsto per Divi nel progetto che proponi: proporre gruppi di scambi che lavorano insieme, mentre l'LP esatto decide quali tenere.

**Prossimi passi:**
1. Aggiungere spostamenti più ampi: scambi tra tre link, più scambi applicati insieme e una perturbazione casuale quando la ricerca riparte. Servono anche come base classica con cui confrontare Divi.
2. Inserire Divi come generatore di proposte: un QUBO sugli scambi possibili attorno ai link congestionati, con i campioni valutati dall'LP. La funzione `propose_moves` è già separata per poterla sostituire.
3. Chiedere ai mentor quanto pesa la scala rispetto alla qualità sulle istanze portfolio senza riferimento. Da questo dipende se restare su network design.

I `.sol` sono ignorati da git, quindi `solutions/` esiste solo in locale. Non ho fatto nessun commit. Ho salvato in memoria la scelta della traccia e la domanda per i mentor.

[package]
name = "check_network"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2021"

[dependencies]
regex = "1.11.1"
# QOBLIB Network Design Solution Checker

This program is part of **QOBLIB - Quantum Optimization Benchmarking Library** and is designed to **verify solutions** to *Network Design Problems*. It checks whether a proposed network topology satisfies degree constraints and correctly routes flows according to demand.

## Problem Description

Design a network with N nodes (between 5 and 24) where each node has exactly two incoming and two outgoing connections. The objective is to minimize the maximum aggregate flow on any edge while routing traffic according to a demand matrix.

## What This Checker Does

Given an instance size, demand matrix, and solution file, this checker:

1. **Parses** the Gurobi-format solution file.
2. **Validates** degree constraints (each node has exactly 2 in-edges and 2 out-edges).
3. **Verifies** flow conservation for each commodity at each node.
4. **Checks** that flows only use existing edges.
5. **Computes** the maximum aggregate flow and verifies it matches the objective.

This program does **not** check for optimality.

## Input Format

### Solution File

The checker reads Gurobi solution files with the following format:

```
# Solution for model obj
# Objective value = 65500
z 65500
x#1#5 0
x#1#4 0
x#1#3 1
...
f#1#2#5 21000
f#1#2#4 0
...
```

Where:
- `z` is the objective value (maximum flow on any edge, scaled by 1000)
- `x#i#j` is 1 if there's an edge from node i to node j, 0 otherwise
- `f#k#i#j` is the amount of flow for commodity k on edge (i,j), scaled by 1000

## Usage

### Building

First, build the checker using Cargo:

```bash
cargo build --release
```

### Command

```bash
./target/release/check_network <instance_size> <demand_file> <solution_file>
```

# PDF Processing Guide

## Overview

This guide covers essential PDF processing operations using Python libraries and command-line tools. For advanced features, JavaScript libraries, and detailed examples, see REFERENCE.md. If you need to fill out a PDF form, read FORMS.md and follow its instructions.

## Quick Start

```python
from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter

# Read a PDF
reader = PdfReader("document.pdf")
print(f"Pages: {len(reader.pages)}")

# Extract text
text = ""
for page in reader.pages:
    text += page.extract_text()
```

## Python Libraries

### pypdf - Basic Operations

#### Merge PDFs
```python
from pypdf import PdfWriter, PdfReader

writer = PdfWriter()
for pdf_file in ["doc1.pdf", "doc2.pdf", "doc3.pdf"]:
    reader = PdfReader(pdf_file)
    for page in reader.pages:
        writer.add_page(page)

with open("merged.pdf", "wb") as output:
    writer.write(output)
```

#### Split PDF
```python
reader = PdfReader("input.pdf")
for i, page in enumerate(reader.pages):
    writer = PdfWriter()
    writer.add_page(page)
    with open(f"page_{i+1}.pdf", "wb") as output:
        writer.write(output)
```

#### Extract Metadata
```python
reader = PdfReader("document.pdf")
meta = reader.metadata
print(f"Title: {meta.title}")
print(f"Author: {meta.author}")
print(f"Subject: {meta.subject}")
print(f"Creator: {meta.creator}")
```

#### Rotate Pages
```python
reader = PdfReader("input.pdf")
writer = PdfWriter()

page = reader.pages[0]
page.rotate(90)  # Rotate 90 degrees clockwise
writer.add_page(page)

with open("rotated.pdf", "wb") as output:
    writer.write(output)
```

### pdfplumber - Text and Table Extraction

#### Extract Text with Layout
```python
import pdfplumber

with pdfplumber.open("document.pdf") as pdf:
    for page in pdf.pages:
        text = page.extract_text()
        print(text)
```

#### Extract Tables
```python
with pdfplumber.open("document.pdf") as pdf:
    for i, page in enumerate(pdf.pages):
        tables = page.extract_tables()
        for j, table in enumerate(tables):
            print(f"Table {j+1} on page {i+1}:")
            for row in table:
                print(row)
```

#### Advanced Table Extraction
```python
import pandas as pd

with pdfplumber.open("document.pdf") as pdf:
    all_tables = []
    for page in pdf.pages:
        tables = page.extract_tables()
        for table in tables:
            if table:  # Check if table is not empty
                df = pd.DataFrame(table[1:], columns=table[0])
                all_tables.append(df)

# Combine all tables
if all_tables:
    combined_df = pd.concat(all_tables, ignore_index=True)
    combined_df.to_excel("extracted_tables.xlsx", index=False)
```

### reportlab - Create PDFs

#### Basic PDF Creation
```python
from reportlab.lib.pagesizes import letter
from reportlab.pdfgen import canvas

c = canvas.Canvas("hello.pdf", pagesize=letter)
width, height = letter

# Add text
c.drawString(100, height - 100, "Hello World!")
c.drawString(100, height - 120, "This is a PDF created with reportlab")

# Add a line
c.line(100, height - 140, 400, height - 140)

# Save
c.save()
```

#### Create PDF with Multiple Pages
```python
from reportlab.lib.pagesizes import letter
from reportlab.platypus import SimpleDocTemplate, Paragraph, Spacer, PageBreak
from reportlab.lib.styles import getSampleStyleSheet

doc = SimpleDocTemplate("report.pdf", pagesize=letter)
styles = getSampleStyleSheet()
story = []

# Add content
title = Paragraph("Report Title", styles['Title'])
story.append(title)
story.append(Spacer(1, 12))

body = Paragraph("This is the body of the report. " * 20, styles['Normal'])
story.append(body)
story.append(PageBreak())

# Page 2
story.append(Paragraph("Page 2", styles['Heading1']))
story.append(Paragraph("Content for page 2", styles['Normal']))

# Build PDF
doc.build(story)
```

#### Subscripts and Superscripts

**IMPORTANT**: Never use Unicode subscript/superscript characters (₀₁₂₃₄₅₆₇₈₉, ⁰¹²³⁴⁵⁶⁷⁸⁹) in ReportLab PDFs. The built-in fonts do not include these glyphs, causing them to render as solid black boxes.

Instead, use ReportLab's XML markup tags in Paragraph objects:
```python
from reportlab.platypus import Paragraph
from reportlab.lib.styles import getSampleStyleSheet

styles = getSampleStyleSheet()

# Subscripts: use <sub> tag
chemical = Paragraph("H<sub>2</sub>O", styles['Normal'])

# Superscripts: use <super> tag
squared = Paragraph("x<super>2</super> + y<super>2</super>", styles['Normal'])
```

For canvas-drawn text (not Paragraph objects), manually adjust font the size and position rather than using Unicode subscripts/superscripts.

## Command-Line Tools

### pdftotext (poppler-utils)
```bash
# Extract text
pdftotext input.pdf output.txt

# Extract text preserving layout
pdftotext -layout input.pdf output.txt

# Extract specific pages
pdftotext -f 1 -l 5 input.pdf output.txt  # Pages 1-5
```

### qpdf
```bash
# Merge PDFs
qpdf --empty --pages file1.pdf file2.pdf -- merged.pdf

# Split pages
qpdf input.pdf --pages . 1-5 -- pages1-5.pdf
qpdf input.pdf --pages . 6-10 -- pages6-10.pdf

# Rotate pages
qpdf input.pdf output.pdf --rotate=+90:1  # Rotate page 1 by 90 degrees

# Remove password
qpdf --password=mypassword --decrypt encrypted.pdf decrypted.pdf
```

### pdftk (if available)
```bash
# Merge
pdftk file1.pdf file2.pdf cat output merged.pdf

# Split
pdftk input.pdf burst

# Rotate
pdftk input.pdf rotate 1east output rotated.pdf
```

## Common Tasks

### Extract Text from Scanned PDFs
```python
# Requires: pip install pytesseract pdf2image
import pytesseract
from pdf2image import convert_from_path

# Convert PDF to images
images = convert_from_path('scanned.pdf')

# OCR each page
text = ""
for i, image in enumerate(images):
    text += f"Page {i+1}:\n"
    text += pytesseract.image_to_string(image)
    text += "\n\n"

print(text)
```

### Add Watermark
```python
from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter

# Create watermark (or load existing)
watermark = PdfReader("watermark.pdf").pages[0]

# Apply to all pages
reader = PdfReader("document.pdf")
writer = PdfWriter()

for page in reader.pages:
    page.merge_page(watermark)
    writer.add_page(page)

with open("watermarked.pdf", "wb") as output:
    writer.write(output)
```

### Extract Images
```bash
# Using pdfimages (poppler-utils)
pdfimages -j input.pdf output_prefix

# This extracts all images as output_prefix-000.jpg, output_prefix-001.jpg, etc.
```

### Password Protection
```python
from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter

reader = PdfReader("input.pdf")
writer = PdfWriter()

for page in reader.pages:
    writer.add_page(page)

# Add password
```

Base directory for this skill: /tmp/claude-1000/bundled-skills/2.1.330/4934d9d1f4f28cc9e9fa02b27183f323/dataviz

# Data Visualization

A chart is **read by people and executed by you**. This skill turns "make it look
good" into a procedure with checks, so the result is right by construction rather
than by taste.

**The method here is design-system-agnostic.** Nothing in the procedure, the form
heuristic, the six checks, or the mark specs is specific to one product. A design
system supplies a small set of *parameters* (its ramps, a categorical order, a
diverging pair, a status palette, a texture, its surfaces, its filter components);
the method consumes them unchanged. A **validated default palette** is the
reference instance, fully specified in `references/palette.md`. To target your
brand, read that file's structure and substitute its values - touch nothing else.

> The single most important habit: **the color part is computable, so compute it.**
> Never eyeball whether a palette is colorblind-safe - run `scripts/validate_palette.js`.

## The procedure - do these in order

Color comes LAST. Most bad charts pick colors first.

1. **Pick the form.** What is the data's job - magnitude, identity, polarity, a
   single headline, change-over-time? The job picks the chart type, and sometimes
   the answer is *not a chart* (a stat tile or hero number). -> `references/choosing-a-form.md`
2. **Assign color by the job it does.** Categorical (identity), sequential
   (magnitude), diverging (polarity), or status (state) - each has one rule.
   Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled. -> `references/color-formula.md`
3. **VALIDATE the palette - run the script, don't reason about Delta E.**
   `node scripts/validate_palette.js "<hex,hex,...>" --mode light` (relative to
   this skill's base directory - or load it as `<script type="module">` in the
   chart's own page, where it reads
   `data-palette` off `<body>` and logs a `console.table` report). It returns
   pass/fail on the lightness band, chroma floor, adjacent-pair CVD separation,
   the normal-vision floor, and contrast. Fix anything that FAILs before continuing. Re-run for
   `--mode dark` with that mode's surface.
4. **Apply mark specs & spacers.** Thin marks, 4px rounded data-ends anchored to
   the baseline, 2px lines, >=8px markers, a 2px surface gap between fills (stacked
   segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring on overlapping marks,
   selective direct labels. -> `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`
5. **Add the hover layer - by default.** An HTML/SVG chart *is* interactive; ship
   a crosshair+tooltip on line/area and a per-mark hover tooltip on bar/dot/cell.
   The only form that skips it is a bare stat tile with no plot. Hit targets bigger
   than the mark; filters in one row above the charts. -> `references/interaction.md`
6. **Final accessibility pass.** For >= 2 series a legend is always present and <= 4
   are also direct-labeled (a single series needs no legend box - the title names
   it), so identity is never color-alone; a table view exists; dark mode is **selected** - its own
   steps from the same ramps, validated against the dark surface, not an automatic
   flip; texture is available for the CVD/print/forced-colors case.
   One exception to direct name labels: the tall segmented bar (*Figures* in `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`).
7. **Render it and look at it.** The validator checks color, not layout - open or
   screenshot the output and eyeball it for label collisions, geometry, and overflow
   before calling it done.

Then check the result against **`references/anti-patterns.md`** - it is the catalog
of what goes wrong. If your chart matches an entry, it's wrong.

## Non-negotiables (true in every design system)

- **Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled.** A 9th series is never a
  generated hue - it folds into "Other," small multiples, or composite encoding.
- **One axis.** Never a dual-axis chart (two y-scales). Two measures of different
  scale -> two charts, small multiples, or indexed to a common base. *(This is the
  #1 chart mistake - see anti-patterns.)*
- **Color follows the entity, never its rank.** A filter that changes the series
  count must not repaint the survivors.
- **Sequential = one hue, light->dark. Diverging = two hues + a neutral gray
  midpoint.** Never a rainbow; never a hue at the diverging midpoint.
- **Run the validator before shipping any categorical palette.** CVD Delta E >= 8 is the
  target (OKLab ×100); 6-8 is a floor that is legal ONLY with secondary encoding. A
  normal-vision floor below 15 is a hard FAIL - full-color readers can't tell the
  pair apart; re-step it on the adjacent pairlist (secondary encoding does not excuse
  this one); under `--pairs all` cut series or facet instead - see check 4. A contrast WARN
  obligates visible labels or a table view - it is not dismissable.
- **Thin marks; a legend always present for >= 2 series (none for one), with
  selective direct labels (never a number on every point); recessive grid/axes.**
  One exception, legend kept: the tall segmented bar (*Figures* in `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`).
- **Text wears text tokens, never the series color** - values, labels, and legends
  stay in primary/secondary/muted ink; a colored mark beside them carries identity.
- **Status colors are reserved** (good/warning/serious/critical) and never reused
  for "series 4"; they ship with an icon + label, never color alone.

## Plugging in a design system

The method is invariant; only these parameters change per system. The reference
instance - every value filled in - is `references/palette.md`.

| Parameter | What the system provides |
|---|---|
| **Ramps** | the hue scales (named steps) the palette draws from |
| **Categorical theme** | the fixed hue order (a named theme); default + alternates |
| **Sequential hue** | the default single hue for magnitude |
| **Diverging pair** | two warm/cool poles + a neutral midpoint |
| **Status palette** | good / warning / serious / critical - steps distinct from categorical, except that dark-mode good is the series green |
| **Texture fill** | one directional hand-drawn fill, used at 45° / 135° |
| **Surfaces** | light & dark chart-surface colors (the validator needs these) |
| **Filter controls** | date-range & dimension controls (behavioral spec in `interaction.md`) |

To onboard a new system: fill those rows, feed its ramps to the validator, and let
it snap each slot to the nearest passing step. Structure and rules stay as written.

## Reference files

| File | What it answers |
|------|-----------------|
| `references/choosing-a-form.md` | Which chart type / is it even a chart? |
| `references/color-formula.md` | The four jobs, the six checks, snap-to-passing |
| `references/marks-and-anatomy.md` | Mark specs, spacers, labels, figures, hero number |
| `references/interaction.md` | Tooltips & hover, filters & time ranges |
| `references/components.md` | The pieces a chart is made of - build each in plain HTML |
| `references/anti-patterns.md` | **What goes wrong - check every chart against this** |
| `references/palette.md` | **The reference palette instance** - every parameter, filled in; swap for your brand's |
| `scripts/validate_palette.js` | Runnable six-checks validator (run it; don't eyeball) |

Scritto per: il team e i mentor/giuria Qoro.

Il PDF è pronto: [network24_report.pdf](network24_report.pdf), 2 pagine A4, in italiano. Contiene:

- **Risultato in evidenza:** 657 121, cioè −0,99% rispetto al best known QOBLIB, con la verifica del checker ufficiale in Rust.
- **Il problema e il metodo,** in breve: una ricerca propone le topologie, l'LP esatto le valuta, e un file si salva solo se passa il checker.
- **Il grafico dell'andamento dello score,** con le cinque fasi in una tabella.
- **Cosa ha funzionato,** con i numeri: le proposte guidate nel parallel tempering, il passo profondo dell'ILS e l'LP incrementale.
- **Il ruolo di Divi** come risultato negativo misurato: il confronto fra QAOA a 16 qubit, simulated annealing, enumerazione esatta e scelta casuale. Il PDF dice esplicitamente che lo score finale viene tutto dalla ricerca classica.
- **Verifiche e limiti,** e i comandi per riprodurre.

Il file è nella cartella del repo, non è in commit, e git non lo ignora. Lo script che lo genera è `/tmp/claude-1000/-home-danie-quantum-icing-qoro/baa491bc-203d-427a-a1d9-f25fcc582a10/scratchpad/make_report.py`, e legge i `log.csv`.

content.text:
Ho aggiunto al PDF la sezione **"I metodi, in breve"**. È una tabella che spiega in parole semplici come funziona ogni metodo e come l'abbiamo usato:

| Metodo | In una riga |
|---|---|
| Ricerca locale | piccole modifiche, si tiene solo ciò che migliora; si blocca in un minimo locale |
| Simulated annealing | accetta a volte anche peggioramenti, con una "temperatura" che scende nel tempo |
| **Parallel tempering** | più copie della ricerca a temperature diverse, che ogni tanto si scambiano le soluzioni: le calde esplorano, le fredde rifiniscono |
| Ricerca locale iterata (ILS) | discesa, poi un "calcio" di mosse casuali, poi di nuovo discesa |
| Passo profondo | invece del calcio, si riparte da tutti i vicini che peggiorano di poco |
| QAOA con Divi | circuito quantistico con parametri regolati da un ottimizzatore classico, per campionare soluzioni di un QUBO |

Ho anche tolto dalla sezione "Cosa ha funzionato" la spiegazione del passo profondo, che ora sarebbe stata ripetuta. Inoltre la tabella di Divi non si spezza più tra due pagine.

Il PDF è passato da 2 a 3 pagine. Il file è sempre [network24_report.pdf](network24_report.pdf).
fai anche la versione in inglese e differenziala con un _eng
